title: Complete Erdős Problem #352 — Triangles of Area 1 in Measurable Sets

problemStatement.formal: \exists\, c > 0 \ \ \text{such that}\ \ \forall\, A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\ \text{measurable with}\ \lambda(A) \ge c,\ \ \exists\, x,y,z \in A\ \text{with}\ \operatorname{area}(\triangle xyz) = 1.
problemStatement.plain: If a region of the plane is "big enough" (has Lebesgue measure at least some universal constant $c$), must it contain three of its own points forming a triangle of area exactly $1$? Erdős conjectured yes, with the smallest sufficient area being $4\pi/\sqrt{27}$.
